items.stem: The smallest natural number is
items.explanation: Natural numbers are the counting numbers, which begin at one.

options.why: Zero is a whole number but is not a counting number.
Negative numbers are integers, not natural numbers.
One comes before two in the counting sequence.

items.stem: Which of the following is an integer but not a natural number?
items.explanation: Integers include zero and the negatives, neither of which is a counting number.

options.why: Four is a counting number, so it is natural as well as an integer.
One is the first natural number.
Seven is a counting number, so it is natural as well as an integer.

items.stem: A rational number can always be written as
items.explanation: A rational number is a ratio of two integers with a non-zero denominator.

options.why: That describes an irrational number.
One half is rational but is not a whole number.
Most rationals are not square roots, and many square roots are irrational.

items.stem: Which of the following is irrational?
items.explanation: The square root of two cannot be written as a ratio of integers.

options.why: This equals 2, which is an integer and therefore rational.
This equals three quarters, a ratio of integers.
This is a ratio of two integers, so it is rational.

items.stem: The set of real numbers is made up of
items.explanation: Every real number is either rational or irrational, and the two sets together exhaust the reals.

options.why: This leaves out the irrationals entirely.
This omits negatives, fractions and irrationals.
This omits repeating and non-repeating decimals.

items.stem: The decimal expansion of a rational number is always
items.explanation: A rational number either terminates or settles into a repeating block, and never does neither.

options.why: One third gives 0.333..., which repeats and never ends.
One quarter gives 0.25, which terminates.
That is the signature of an irrational number.

items.stem: Division of any non-zero number by zero is
items.explanation: No number multiplied by zero gives a non-zero result, so the quotient does not exist.

options.why: Zero times any number is zero, not the original number.
One times zero is zero, not the original number.
Infinity is not a number and cannot be the value of a quotient.

items.stem: Between any two distinct rational numbers, the count of rational numbers is
items.explanation: The average of two rationals is rational and lies between them, and the argument repeats without end.

options.why: Averaging again gives another, so one is never the whole story.
The averaging argument never terminates, so no finite bound exists.
The average of the two is itself a rational lying between them.

items.stem: A proof by contradiction begins by assuming
items.explanation: The method assumes the opposite of what is to be proved and derives an impossibility from it.

options.why: Assuming the claim would make the argument circular.
Every proof by contradiction begins from an assumption.
A single example can never establish a general claim.

items.stem: The sum of a rational number and an irrational number is always
items.explanation: If the sum were rational, subtracting the rational part would make the irrational part rational, which is impossible.

options.why: That would force the irrational part to be rational, a contradiction.
One plus the square root of two is neither an integer nor rational.
The contradiction argument rules this out in every case.

items.stem: What are natural numbers?
items.answer: Natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on, used to count objects. They do not include zero or any negative number.

items.stem: Why was the invention of zero important?
items.answer: Zero gave a symbol for nothing and, more importantly, a place holder in positional notation, which is what allows 205 to be distinguished from 25. Without it a positional number system cannot work.

items.stem: What is meant by a one-to-one correspondence between two sets?
items.answer: It is a pairing in which every member of the first set is matched with exactly one member of the second and no member is left out on either side. It is how counting works without using number names.

items.stem: State the type of decimal expansion of 3 divided by 8.
items.answer: Terminating. It equals 0.375, because the denominator 8 is a power of two and so divides a power of ten.

items.stem: Write one rational number lying between 1 by 4 and 1 by 3.
items.answer: Their average is a convenient choice: (1 by 4 plus 1 by 3) divided by 2 equals (7 by 12) divided by 2, which is 7 by 24. Since 7 by 24 is a ratio of integers, it is rational, and it lies between the two.

items.stem: What is a cyclic number?
items.answer: A cyclic number is one whose digits are shifted round in the same cyclic order when it is multiplied by certain whole numbers. The classic example is 142857, from the decimal expansion of one seventh.

items.stem: Why is the product of two irrational numbers not always irrational?
items.answer: Because the irrational parts can cancel. The square root of two times the square root of two is exactly 2, which is rational. So irrationality is not preserved by multiplication, unlike the sum of a rational and an irrational.

items.stem: Can every point on the number line be labelled with a rational number? Justify.
items.answer: No. The point at a distance equal to the square root of two from the origin is a genuine point on the line, and that length is irrational. The rationals leave gaps; only the full set of real numbers fills the line completely.

items.stem: Explain how the number system is extended from natural numbers to integers and then to rational numbers, saying what each extension makes possible.
items.answer: Natural numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on let us count, but subtraction of a larger number from a smaller one has no answer among them. Adding zero and the negatives gives the integers, in which every subtraction is possible. However, division does not always work in the integers, since 3 divided by 2 has no integer answer. Adding all ratios of integers with a non-zero denominator gives the rational numbers, in which every division except by zero is possible. Each extension is made to allow an operation that the previous system could not always perform.

items.stem: State the rules for multiplying and dividing signed numbers, and give one example of each case.
items.answer: A positive times a positive is positive, for example 3 times 4 equals 12. A negative times a negative is positive, for example (-3) times (-4) equals 12. A positive times a negative is negative, for example 3 times (-4) equals -12. The same sign rules hold for division: (-12) divided by (-4) is 3, while (-12) divided by 4 is -3. Brahmagupta set these rules out systematically, describing positives as fortunes and negatives as debts, which makes the sign rules read as sensible statements about money.

items.stem: Convert 0.666... into a fraction, showing your method.
items.answer: Let x equal 0.666... . Multiply both sides by 10, since one digit repeats, giving 10x equal to 6.666... . Subtract the first equation from the second: 10x minus x equals 6.666... minus 0.666..., so 9x equals 6. Therefore x equals 6 by 9, which simplifies to 2 by 3. The method works because multiplying by a power of ten shifts the repeating block so that subtraction removes it entirely.

items.stem: Convert 0.272727... into a fraction, showing your method.
items.answer: Let x equal 0.272727... . Two digits repeat, so multiply by 100, giving 100x equal to 27.272727... . Subtracting gives 100x minus x equals 27, so 99x equals 27 and x equals 27 by 99. Dividing numerator and denominator by 9 gives 3 by 11. The power of ten chosen must match the length of the repeating block, which is why 100 was used here and 10 for a single repeating digit.

items.stem: Find three rational numbers between 1 by 2 and 3 by 4.
items.answer: Write both with a common denominator large enough to leave room: 1 by 2 equals 8 by 16 and 3 by 4 equals 12 by 16. Now 9 by 16, 10 by 16 and 11 by 16 all lie between them, and each is a ratio of integers, so each is rational. Simplifying, 10 by 16 is 5 by 8. The method generalises: choosing a larger common denominator always creates as many gaps as required, which is why infinitely many rationals lie between any two.

items.stem: Explain the structure of a proof by contradiction and why it establishes the original claim.
items.answer: To prove a statement, one assumes its negation and reasons carefully from that assumption until an impossibility is reached, such as a number being both even and odd. Since correct reasoning from a true assumption cannot produce a falsehood, the assumption must have been false. The negation being false means the original statement is true. The method is valuable when the claim is a denial, as with the claim that the square root of two is not a ratio of integers: it is far easier to assume that such a ratio exists and extract a contradiction from it than to examine every possible ratio.

items.stem: Explain how a length equal to the square root of two can be constructed exactly, and what this shows about irrational numbers.
items.answer: Draw a square of side one unit. By the Pythagoras theorem its diagonal has length equal to the square root of (1 squared plus 1 squared), which is the square root of 2. Setting a compass to that diagonal and marking it from the origin along the number line locates the point at the square root of two exactly. This shows that an irrational number is not an approximation or a defect of measurement: it is the exact length of a perfectly ordinary geometrical object. It also shows that the rationals do not fill the number line, since this constructible point carries no rational label.

items.stem: Madhava expressed pi as an infinite series. Discuss what an infinite series can and cannot give us about pi.
items.answer: An infinite series gives a rule for generating better and better approximations: taking more terms brings the running total as close to pi as desired, and it gives a way to bound the error. That is how pi was computed to many places long before machines. What it cannot do is produce pi as a finished decimal, because pi is irrational and its expansion never terminates or repeats, so no finite number of terms is exact. The series is therefore a complete description of pi as a limit while being permanently incomplete as a decimal, and this is the right way to understand every irrational number: exactly specifiable, never exactly writable in decimal form.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Every integer is a rational number. Reason (R): Any integer n can be written as n over 1. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and writing n over 1 is exactly what shows an integer meets the definition of rational.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Being expressible as a ratio of integers is precisely the definition.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: Any integer can indeed be written over a denominator of one.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Integers satisfy the definition of rational numbers.

items.stem: Assertion (A): The square root of every natural number is irrational. Reason (R): The square root of 2 is irrational. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: The reason is true but the assertion is false: the square root of 4 is 2, which is rational, so the claim fails for perfect squares.

options.text: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R explains A
options.why: One example cannot establish a claim about every natural number.

options.text: Both A and R are false
options.why: The square root of 2 is genuinely irrational, so R is true.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The square root of 9 is 3, which is rational, so the assertion fails.

items.stem: Assertion (A): 0.999... equals 1. Reason (R): The two differ by an amount smaller than any positive number. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and a difference smaller than every positive number must be zero, so the two are the same number.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: A difference below every positive bound is exactly what forces equality.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: No positive number is small enough to be the difference.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Letting x equal 0.999... gives 10x = 9 + x, so x = 1.

items.stem: Assertion (A): Between any two real numbers there is an irrational number. Reason (R): The irrationals are dense in the real line. Choose the correct option.
items.explanation: Both are true, and density of the irrationals is exactly the property the assertion states.

options.text: Both A and R are true and R explains A
Both A and R are true but R does not explain A
options.why: Density is precisely the statement that one lies between any two.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.why: The irrationals are genuinely dense in the real line.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.why: Adding a small irrational to the smaller number produces one in between.

items.stem: State whether true or false: zero is a natural number.
items.explanation: Natural numbers are the counting numbers and begin at one.

options.why: Zero is a whole number but is not used for counting objects.

items.stem: State whether true or false: every whole number is a rational number.
items.explanation: Any whole number n can be written as n over 1, a ratio of integers.

options.why: Writing n over 1 satisfies the definition of a rational number.

items.stem: State whether true or false: 22 divided by 7 is equal to pi.
items.explanation: It is a convenient rational approximation, but pi is irrational and the two differ from the third decimal place.

options.why: 22 by 7 is 3.142857..., a rational approximation; pi is 3.14159... and is irrational.

items.stem: State whether true or false: the sum of two irrational numbers is always irrational.
items.explanation: The square root of two plus its negative gives zero, which is rational, so the claim fails.

options.why: Two irrationals can cancel; the square root of 2 plus its negative is zero.

items.stem: The Sanskrit word for zero is ___________.
items.answer: shunya

items.stem: Natural numbers together with zero and the negatives form the ___________.
items.answer: integers

items.stem: A number whose decimal expansion neither terminates nor repeats is ___________.
items.answer: irrational

items.stem: The rational and irrational numbers together make up the ___________ numbers.
items.answer: real

items.stem: Describe the real number system, explaining how each family of numbers sits inside the next and what distinguishes rationals from irrationals.
items.answer: The natural numbers are the counting numbers 1, 2, 3 and so on. Adding zero gives the whole numbers, and adding the negatives gives the integers, so that every subtraction becomes possible. Allowing every ratio of integers with a non-zero denominator gives the rational numbers, so that every division except by zero becomes possible. Each family is contained in the next: every natural number is a whole number, every whole number is an integer, and every integer is rational, since n can be written as n over 1. The rationals do not exhaust the number line. Numbers such as the square root of two and pi cannot be written as a ratio of integers, and these are the irrational numbers. The two families are distinguished cleanly by their decimal expansions: a rational number either terminates, as 0.25 does, or settles into a repeating block, as 0.333... does, while an irrational number neither terminates nor repeats. Together the rationals and the irrationals form the real numbers, and these fill the number line completely, with every point carrying exactly one real label.

items.stem: Explain the method for converting a repeating decimal to a fraction, and use it on 0.1232323... .
items.answer: The method removes the repeating tail by subtraction. Let x be the decimal. Multiply by a power of ten large enough to move the decimal point just past the non-repeating part, and by another power of ten that moves it a full repeating block further. Subtracting the two results makes the identical infinite tails cancel, leaving a finite equation to solve. For x equal to 0.1232323..., the digit 1 does not repeat and the block 23 does. Multiply by 10 to clear the non-repeating digit: 10x equals 1.232323... . Multiply by 1000 to move a further two places: 1000x equals 123.232323... . Subtracting gives 1000x minus 10x equals 123.232323... minus 1.232323..., so 990x equals 122. Therefore x equals 122 by 990, which simplifies by dividing both by 2 to 61 by 495. The result confirms the general fact that any repeating decimal is rational, since the method always ends in a ratio of two integers.

items.stem: Discuss how we know irrational numbers exist, and why their discovery mattered.
items.answer: Their existence is established by proof, not by measurement. The classic argument assumes the square root of two can be written as a fraction p over q in lowest terms and derives a contradiction: squaring gives p squared equal to 2q squared, so p squared is even and hence p is even; writing p as 2k gives 4k squared equal to 2q squared, so q squared is even and q is even too; but then p and q share the factor 2, contradicting lowest terms. Since the assumption leads to an impossibility, no such fraction exists. Geometry then shows the number is perfectly real, because the diagonal of a unit square has exactly that length and can be marked on the number line with a compass. The discovery mattered because it broke the belief that every quantity is a ratio of whole numbers, which had been a foundation of Greek mathematics. It forced a distinction between number and measurement, made the number line rather than the fraction the basic object, and led eventually to a careful treatment of limits and of the real numbers themselves. It also shows the power of proof: a fact about infinitely many possible fractions is settled in a few lines without testing any of them.

items.stem: The rationals are dense in the number line, yet they do not fill it. Explain this apparent paradox.
items.answer: Density means that between any two distinct real numbers, however close, there is a rational number; one can always be found by taking a suitable fraction with a large enough denominator. So the rationals leave no interval, however short, entirely free of them. It is tempting to conclude that they must therefore account for every point. They do not, and the two facts are consistent because they are about different things. Density says the rationals come arbitrarily close to every point; it does not say they land on every point. The square root of two has rationals within a millionth of it, and within a billionth, and yet is not itself any of them, as the contradiction proof shows. A helpful way to see it is that being surrounded arbitrarily closely is not the same as being hit. The irrationals are dense too, and there are in a precise sense far more of them than there are rationals, so the number line is mostly irrational while still having a rational arbitrarily near to every one of its points. The paradox dissolves once approaching a point and occupying it are kept apart, and that distinction is exactly what the idea of a limit was invented to handle.

items.stem: Express 0.4 as a fraction in lowest terms.
items.answer: 0.4 means 4 tenths, so it is 4 by 10. Dividing numerator and denominator by their common factor 2 gives 2 by 5. Since 2 and 5 share no factor other than 1, the fraction 2 by 5 is in lowest terms.

items.stem: Find two rational numbers between 0.2 and 0.3.
items.answer: Write both with more decimal places: 0.200 and 0.300. Then 0.21 and 0.25 both lie between them. As fractions these are 21 by 100 and 1 by 4, each a ratio of integers, so both are rational. Any decimal beginning 0.2 followed by a non-zero digit will do, which is why infinitely many choices exist.

items.stem: A right-angled triangle has legs of 1 unit and 2 units. Find the hypotenuse and state whether it is rational.
items.answer: By the Pythagoras theorem the hypotenuse squared equals 1 squared plus 2 squared, which is 1 plus 4, giving 5. So the hypotenuse is the square root of 5 units. Since 5 is not a perfect square, its square root is irrational: the same contradiction argument used for the square root of two applies, because assuming the square root of 5 equals p over q in lowest terms forces both p and q to be divisible by 5. The length is therefore irrational, yet it is the exact length of an ordinary triangle and can be marked on the number line with a compass.

items.stem: Match each number in Column I with its decimal type in Column II. Column I: (a) 1 by 4, (b) 1 by 3, (c) the square root of 2, (d) 5. Column II: (i) non-terminating non-repeating, (ii) terminating, (iii) non-terminating repeating, (iv) terminating whole number.
items.answer: (a) 1 by 4 - (ii) terminating, since it is 0.25. (b) 1 by 3 - (iii) non-terminating repeating, since it is 0.333... . (c) the square root of 2 - (i) non-terminating non-repeating, since it is irrational. (d) 5 - (iv) terminating whole number, since it is 5.0.

items.stem: Match each number in Column I with the smallest family in Column II that contains it. Column I: (a) 7, (b) -3, (c) 2 by 5, (d) pi. Column II: (i) irrational, (ii) natural, (iii) rational but not an integer, (iv) integer but not natural.
items.answer: (a) 7 - (ii) natural, being a counting number. (b) -3 - (iv) integer but not natural, since negatives are not counting numbers. (c) 2 by 5 - (iii) rational but not an integer, since it is a ratio that does not divide exactly. (d) pi - (i) irrational, since its expansion neither terminates nor repeats.

items.stem: Describe and draw the construction that locates the square root of 2 exactly on the number line.
items.answer: Draw a number line and mark the points 0 and 1. At the point 1, draw a line perpendicular to the number line and mark a point A on it at a distance of one unit from the line, so that the segment from 1 to A is one unit. Join the origin O to A. The triangle O, 1, A is right-angled at the point 1, with both legs one unit, so by the Pythagoras theorem OA equals the square root of (1 plus 1), which is the square root of 2. Now set a compass to the length OA, place its point at the origin and draw an arc cutting the number line to the right. Label that intersection P. Then OP equals the square root of 2, so P is the exact position of the square root of 2 on the line. Label on the diagram the unit square legs, the hypotenuse OA, the compass arc and the point P, and note that the same method with legs 1 and 2 locates the square root of 5.

items.stem: Draw a labelled diagram showing how the families of numbers are nested inside one another, and mark one example in each region.
items.answer: Draw a large rectangle labelled Real Numbers. Inside it draw two regions that together fill it and do not overlap: label the left one Rational Numbers and the right one Irrational Numbers, and mark the square root of 2 and pi in the irrational region. Inside the rational region draw a smaller oval labelled Integers, and inside that a smaller oval labelled Whole Numbers, and inside that a smaller oval labelled Natural Numbers. Mark 3 in the natural oval, 0 in the whole-number ring outside the naturals, -4 in the integer ring outside the whole numbers, and 2 by 5 in the rational region outside the integers. Annotate the diagram with the reason for each nesting: every natural number is whole, every whole number is an integer, and every integer n is rational because it equals n over 1. Add a note that the rational and irrational regions are disjoint and together exhaust the reals, so no real number is both and none is neither.

items.stem: Prove that the square root of 2 is irrational.
items.answer: Suppose, for contradiction, that the square root of 2 is rational. Then it can be written as p over q where p and q are integers, q is not zero, and the fraction is in its lowest terms, so p and q have no common factor other than 1. Squaring both sides of the square root of 2 equals p over q gives 2 equals p squared over q squared, so p squared equals 2 times q squared. The right-hand side is even, so p squared is even. If p were odd then p squared would be odd, so p must be even. Write p as 2k for some integer k. Substituting gives (2k) squared equal to 2 q squared, that is 4 k squared equal to 2 q squared, and dividing by 2 gives q squared equal to 2 k squared. By the same reasoning as before, q squared is even and therefore q is even. So both p and q are even, which means both are divisible by 2. But this contradicts the assumption that p over q was in lowest terms with no common factor. The contradiction shows the original supposition was false. Therefore the square root of 2 cannot be written as a ratio of two integers, and it is irrational. Note that the argument uses nothing about the size of p and q, so it settles the question for all possible fractions at once without testing any of them.
